prompt.context: Our client is a national shipping company that focuses on ground transportation of commercial freight. For the past 15 years, it has been using diesel engines to power its fleet of vehicles, but now wants to explore the possibility of switching to electric powered engines (EV technology) due to rising fuel costs. The CEO has approached us for guidance and wants to know how to proceed.
prompt.question: Should the client switch its fleet from diesel to electric (EV) engines? How would you approach evaluating this decision?

clarifying_info.q: Has the client identified an EV supplier?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, the client has identified a supplier to provide the electric vehicle technology since it does not have in-house capabilities.

clarifying_info.q: Would the client buy new vehicles or retrofit existing ones?
clarifying_info.a: The client wants to retrofit existing vehicles rather than buying new ones, given its extensive fleet.

clarifying_info.q: Has any other ground transportation company switched to EV?
clarifying_info.a: No. If the client proceeds, it will be the first in the industry to do so.

clarifying_info.q: What is the size of the fleet?
What is the fuel tank size per vehicle?
What is the average miles per gallon (current diesel)?
What is the cost of fuel per gallon?
How many miles does each vehicle travel per week on average?
What is the annual maintenance and repair cost per vehicle (current)?
What is the insurance cost per vehicle per year (current)?
What is the labor cost per vehicle per year?
What would the EV mpg equivalent be?
clarifying_info.a: EV technology has the potential to double existing fuel efficiency, so 20 mpg equivalent.

clarifying_info.q: What would maintenance/repair costs be under EV?
What would insurance cost under EV?
What is the cost to retrofit one vehicle?
What is the remaining useful life of the current vehicles?
Can we assume the current supplier is the best option?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, assume the current supplier offers the best EV opportunity in terms of price and efficiency.

exhibits.title: Costs Page
exhibits.shows: A two-column table comparing breakdown of current costs and future costs per vehicle, listing number of vehicles, fuel tank size, average mpg, cost of fuel per gallon, average miles travelled per week, average annual maintenance and repair, insurance, and labor.

framework: Revenue impact: assess whether EV adoption improves business relationships, reduces carbon footprint for supply-chain partners, or enables pricing premiums
Costs: compare all per-vehicle cost line items (fuel, maintenance, insurance, labor) under diesel vs. EV; calculate initial retrofit investment and payback period
Competitive / industry dynamics: first-mover advantage could drive market share gains; failure to implement could cede ground to rivals if EV becomes standard
Execution / capability risk: company has no prior EV experience (learning curve); being first to test the technology adds unproven-technology risk
Feasibility check: net lifetime savings per vehicle vs. retrofit cost determines whether the switch is economically justified

questions.prompt: Calculate current annual fuel cost per vehicle
questions.guidance: Strong candidates will structure the calculation step by step: miles per tank, fill-ups per week, weekly cost, then annualise. Bonus for noting that doubling efficiency halves fuel spend without re-deriving.

math.setup: Miles per tank = mpg × tank size; fill-ups/week = weekly miles ÷ miles per tank; weekly fuel cost = fill-ups × tank size × price/gallon; annual cost ≈ weekly cost × 50 weeks
steps: Miles per tank = 10 mpg × 50 gal = 500 miles

questions.prompt: Calculate future (EV) annual fuel cost per vehicle
questions.guidance: Candidates who recognise that doubling mpg halves fuel cost should receive bonus credit. Otherwise walk through the same structure.

math.setup: Same structure as current, but mpg = 20
steps: Miles per tank = 20 mpg × 50 gal = 1,000 miles

questions.prompt: Calculate total annual cost per vehicle under current diesel and under EV, then determine annual savings
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify which cost lines change (fuel, maintenance, insurance) and which stay the same (labor). Arrive at net annual saving of $2,500 per vehicle.

math.setup: Sum all per-vehicle annual cost items for each scenario

questions.prompt: Calculate net lifetime savings per vehicle and total fleet-level savings, given the $5,000 retrofit cost and 10-year remaining useful life
questions.guidance: Multiply annual saving by remaining useful life, then subtract retrofit investment. Scale to fleet. Bonus points for mentioning time value of money / NPV.

math.setup: Lifetime saving per vehicle = annual saving × years − retrofit cost; fleet saving = per-vehicle saving × number of vehicles
steps: Lifetime fuel/cost saving per vehicle = $2,500 × 10 years = $25,000
Net saving per vehicle after retrofit = $25,000 − $5,000 = $20,000
math.answer: $40 million net savings over the remaining useful life of the fleet

brainstorming.prompt: What risks should the client consider before proceeding with the EV conversion?

categories.name: Technology risk
ideas: Client is first in industry — EV effectiveness in commercial freight is unproven
Current EV technology is largely designed for short-range use; vehicles must commute 1,000 miles per week
Limited recharging infrastructure across the US could disrupt operations

categories.name: Implementation / operational risk
ideas: No in-house EV expertise creates a steep learning curve
Fleet-wide failure or downtime could allow competitors to capture market share
Retrofit process may temporarily reduce available fleet capacity

categories.name: Financial / cost risk
ideas: Maintenance and insurance costs increase significantly under EV
There may be unanticipated costs (charging infrastructure, driver training, warranty issues)
Time value of money reduces the real value of long-horizon savings

categories.name: Supplier / dependency risk
ideas: Client relies entirely on a single external supplier for EV technology
Supplier failure, price changes, or technology updates could strand the investment

categories.name: Regulatory / incentive uncertainty
ideas: Government incentives for EV adoption may or may not be available
Future environmental regulations could accelerate or change requirements

recommendation: The client should proceed with retrofitting its fleet to EV technology. The conversion generates net savings of $40 million over the remaining 10-year useful life of the fleet — a strong financial case for switching.
risks: First-mover risk: EV technology is untested in commercial freight and current systems are designed for short-range use
Limited US recharging infrastructure could disrupt 1,000-miles-per-week operations
Higher maintenance ($3,500 vs. $500) and insurance ($3,000 vs. $1,000) costs partially offset fuel savings
No in-house EV expertise requires investment in training and change management
Unanticipated costs could erode projected savings
next_steps: Run a pilot with a small subset of vehicles to validate EV performance under real commercial freight conditions
Work closely with the supplier to establish support, SLAs, and contingency plans
Survey driver base for feedback on EV operability and range concerns
Research federal and state government incentives for commercial EV adoption
Assess feasibility of installing proprietary charging stations at key depots to reduce reliance on public infrastructure
Investigate whether EV adoption can be marketed to customers as a sustainability differentiator to grow revenue
